claims.text: The initial composite contains discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
Untreated W–Cu composites undergo phase separation under operational thermal cycling and irradiation.
Untreated W–Cu composites form interfacial voids under operational thermal cycling and irradiation.
An Mo interlayer a few nanometers thick can be deposited on W surfaces before composite assembly.
The deposited Mo interlayer creates a chemically graded W–Mo–Cu interface.
The Mo interlayer bonds well with both W and Cu.
The Mo interlayer reduces W–Cu interfacial energy.
The Mo interlayer promotes a coherent, continuous phase across the W–Cu interface.
Mo has good wetting behavior with both W and Cu.
Interfacial Mo enhances atomic diffusion and bonding during heat treatment.
Enhanced interfacial diffusion and bonding reduce the thermodynamic driving force for Cu dewetting and phase separation.
Under irradiation, the Mo layer helps fill developing interfacial voids.
Suppression or filling of interfacial voids maintains a continuous thermal-conduction path.
Mo-treated W–Cu composites will exhibit fewer interfacial voids than untreated composites under matched thermal and irradiation exposure.
Mo-treated W–Cu composites will exhibit less phase separation than untreated composites under matched thermal and irradiation exposure.
Mo-treated W–Cu composites will retain higher and more stable thermal conductivity than untreated composites under matched thermal and irradiation exposure.
Void formation and phase separation at conventional W–Cu interfaces undermine thermal transport and long-term reliability.
The proposed effect is applicable to W–Cu joints exposed to temperatures and irradiation environments comparable to accelerated aging tests for plasma-facing and cooling components.
